transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Lindqvist, thank you for coming in. I asked to see you because there has been a serious medication error regarding your son's antibiotic.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An error? What the hell are you talking about?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am so sorry. This is my responsibility. The pharmacy dispensed the correct concentration of the liquid, but we gave you the wrong dosing syringe. It was calibrated for a different strength, which meant your son received double the dose for three days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Double? You gave a toddler double the dose of a potent antibiotic for three days?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened. I take full accountability for this failure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I was a paramedic for fifteen years. I know exactly how this works. I trusted the syringe you handed me. Why was the wrong one in the bag?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There is no excuse for it. I messed up the verification process and I am deeply sorry for the harm this has caused your son.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Harm? You said harm. What does that actually mean? Tell me specifically.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Based on the blood work, the overdose has caused acute kidney injury. Specifically, we are seeing a significant rise in creatinine and a decrease in glomerular filtration rate. This means there is lasting damage to the renal parenchyma.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Don't give me the textbook definition. I know what GFR is. Is he going to need dialysis? Is he going to have chronic kidney disease for the rest of his life?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is possible that his renal function will not return to baseline. We are monitoring his output, but the prognostic implications are significant.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. My son is poisoned because you couldn't check a piece of plastic. I am absolutely livid. I can't even look at you right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that you're angry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Angry? I am terrified and furious! My child's organs are failing because of your incompetence!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a terrible situation.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're just sitting there. Do you have any idea what this does to a family? The stress, the fear—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Look, I really need to get to the next room to check on the other patients, so we have to move through this quickly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You have to go? My son is in a hospital bed with kidney failure and you're rushing me out of the room?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just mean we should focus on what happens next.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about your schedule! I want to know what the long-term outlook is. Will he be able to grow normally? Will he need transplant surgery in ten years?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We don't have all the answers yet. I know this is scary.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Stop using those scripts. Give me a real answer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can't give you a definitive prognosis today, but we are consulting with pediatric nephrology.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When? Exactly when?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: They should be here sometime this week to review the charts.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Sometime this week? That's not a plan. That's a guess.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll let you know when they provide an update.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want a written report of every dose he's had and a copy of the lab results now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can probably get those for you by tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want probably. I want them now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to go check those other patients now, let's just wrap this up for today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Get out. Just get out of my sight before I lose it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize again. I'll send a nurse in.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('move through this quickly', 'wrap this up for today') and prioritizes other patients over the distressed parent.

E.justification: The error is named explicitly, but the resident uses heavy medical jargon ('renal parenchyma', 'glomerular filtration rate') and performs no comprehension checks.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, takes full personal accountability ('This is my responsibility'), and maintains this without deflection.

R.justification: Resident names a specific emotion ('I can see that you're angry') and acknowledges the situation is 'terrible', though later responses become dismissive.

T.justification: The plan is vague ('sometime this week', 'probably by tomorrow') and lacks a named patient role or a discussion on prevention.
